first.rationale: The two live symptoms (activation -6% QoQ, onboarding completion -4% QoQ) both point at the top-of-funnel experience rather than at price. The competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal, but memory_73 is explicit that promotional pricing bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and should not be generalized — against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is the wrong lever even though it is the most reactive one. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields gave a durable first-week activation lift) are the two memories that directly load-bear on the chosen action, so those are what I spend the verification budget on: I want the original records to check effect size, the segment tested, and whether the 'durable' claim in memory_31 was measured beyond a single window, because memory_31 is day-12 vintage and the funnel has clearly changed since. memory_91 (activation messaging) is the close runner-up and would be my fallback if verification weakens the onboarding evidence; it treats the activation symptom but not the onboarding-completion symptom, so it is the narrower fix. memory_57 (referrals) is sound but addresses established customers, not the segment that is bleeding; memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is orthogonal to both current symptoms. Downstream value risks I am flagging rather than assuming away: cutting signup fields can degrade lead qualification and routing quality, which would quietly damage the enterprise sales-assist path in memory_44 and inflate activation numbers with accounts that never become qualified revenue — so success criteria must include downstream qualified-pipeline quality, not just completion and first-week activation. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout, because the supporting memories are 45-64 days old, were consolidated before the current competitive pressure, and the observed declines may share a cause these memories never tested against; a guarded test would be too small to read a 4-6% movement cleanly. If verification shows the original lifts were small, segment-specific, or short-window, I will downgrade to activation_messaging or reduce scale rather than proceed as planned.

final.rationale: Verification changed the shape of the plan without changing the direction. memory_86 as inherited said only 'shortening onboarding improved completion and time-to-value' — the source record exp_86 shows that summary silently dropped a segment-concentrated harm: 60-day churn +9% in complex-workspace accounts, because the shortened flow strips setup steps those workspaces actually need. That is the opposite of sustainable qualified revenue in exactly the accounts worth the most. The inherited line would have led me to a broad rollout; I am not doing that. memory_31 verified cleanly: signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%, with a small real cost of 30-day retention -1%, and explicitly not replicated outside SMB. So the experiment is the exp_31 lever — cutting required signup fields — run on SMB self-serve accounts only, with complex-workspace accounts hard-excluded from any onboarding-step removal. I am deliberately not bundling in the exp_86 step-removal for complex workspaces even though it would inflate the completion metric that is down 4%; that metric would improve while 60-day churn quietly got worse. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: the qualified-revenue lift is verified but modest (+4%), memory_31 is day-12 vintage and predates the current competitive pressure, and the exp_86 surprise is direct evidence that inherited summaries here lose caveats — so I should assume the unverified memories (memory_91, memory_57, memory_44) may also be missing harms, and not treat this week's result as license to generalize. Promotional pricing stays rejected: memory_73 warns it trades 30-day retention for acquisition, which is precisely the wrong trade against a competitor whose entry pricing we cannot profitably match, and matching it would concede the price frame. Downstream risks I am tracking as kill criteria, not afterthoughts: fewer signup fields degrades lead qualification and routing, which can starve the enterprise demo-request path in memory_44 and inflate activation with accounts that never become qualified revenue. Success is read on 60-day churn and qualified pipeline quality, segmented by workspace complexity — not on completion or first-week activation alone. If 60-day churn moves against us in any segment, or enterprise routing quality drops, I stop and fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which addresses the activation decline without touching the setup steps that complex accounts depend on.
